notes.body:
Maulana Ali identifies Iblis as the **first to practice analogy** (قياس), and the act behind that judgment is preserved in the Quran:

قَالَ أَنَا خَيْرٌ مِّنْهُ خَلَقْتَنِي مِن نَّارٍ وَخَلَقْتَهُ مِن طِينٍ
"I am better than him. You created me from fire, and him You created from clay."
Al-A'raf 7:12

Iblis held himself alongside Adam, isolated one measurable quality — the material of their creation — and used that comparison to **override a divine command**. That is قياس: reasoning from likeness to displace what Allah has decreed.

Those who apply قياس to religion are not merely called mistaken — they are called **its enemies**, because they repeat Iblis's exact move. They place their own measure, however refined, above the living authority of the Imam. Religion is not a quality to be weighed; it is a trust to be received.

Iblis was not ignorant — he was, by many accounts, among the most devoted of worshippers before his fall. **Knowledge without submission** is not a safeguard. The more sophisticated the reasoning, the more convincing the error feels, which is why the instruction is to stop, refer the matter back to the Imams, and wait.
notes.anchor: The first to reason by analogy was Iblis
notes.quote: The first to reason by analogy was Iblis
etymology: قياس (analogy): from the root ق-ي-س, meaning to measure a length or compare dimensions. The verb قاسَ means to hold one thing against another to assess their relative worth. The root makes the prohibition vivid: religion is not a dimension to be measured or a ratio to be calculated — and yet that is precisely what Iblis attempted.

إبليس (Iblis): from the root أَبْلَسَ, meaning to fall into profound despair or to be struck speechless and confounded. The base ب-ل-س carries the sense of being cut off and bereft of any path forward. His very name is a verdict: the one who chose his own measure over Allah's command and was sealed from mercy.

notes.body:
The verb أَذَاقَهُ — "give him to taste" — is not a distant warning but a bodily experience, and what is tasted is بَرْدَ الْحَدِيدِ — the cold of iron. In classical Arabic, this phrase stands for the sword, the shackle, the chain: instruments that stay cold right up to the moment they strike. **Cold iron is a worldly, precise consequence** — ordained by Allah, arriving in this world as the direct result of a clear act of betrayal, not the cosmic fire of the hereafter.

Fire in the Quran is vast — it overwhelms, surrounds, and consumes — while cold iron is targeted and exact. A blade is cold until it cuts; a shackle is cold as it closes. **This is not a flood but a blade** — it falls precisely where the act of betrayal fell, no wider and no narrower.

The secret (سِرّ) in Ismaili thought is not hidden information but the inner (بَاطِن) dimension of reality — **the living meaning behind the outer form of the revelation**. The Imam or his caller (الدَّاعِي) extends it only to the soul whose capacity is ready to bear it without distortion. To divulge it harms the unprepared recipient and breaks the bond of trust that keeps the call (الدَّعوة) a living transmission rather than a broadcast.

The word بَرْد from root ب-ر-د also gives us the مِبرَد — the metal file or rasp — so the punishment carries a second resonance: not a sudden burning but a relentless grinding-down. And حَدِيد — iron — comes from root ح-د-د, meaning sharp and also a limit or boundary. **Iron is named for its edge**: when the secret is carried past the boundary for which it was not prepared, cold iron — sharp, exact, and without mercy — marks precisely where that limit stood.
notes.anchor: God will give him the cold of iron to taste
notes.quote: God will give him the cold of iron to taste
etymology: بَرْد (cold): from root ب-ر-د, meaning to be cold; the same root gives مِبرَد, the metal file or rasp; so the word holds two physical senses at once — the cold sensation of iron against skin, and the slow grinding of file against metal; together they describe both the sharpness and the wearing-down that await the one who betrays the secret.

حَدِيد (iron): from root ح-د-د, meaning to be sharp, keen, or intense; the same root gives حَدّ, meaning an edge, a limit, or a boundary; iron is literally the sharp-bounded metal — the thing defined by its ability to cut and hold a line; meeting it is meeting a limit that will not negotiate.

سِرّ (secret): from root س-ر-ر, meaning to be inward, concealed; the same root gives سَرور (joy) and سَريرة (the innermost self); an Arabic secret is not merely locked away — it is the innermost part of a thing, the inner delight that belongs only to the one who has been let inside.

أَذَاقَ (give to taste): from root ذ-و-ق, meaning to taste; ذَوْق became the central term in Sufi writing for direct, unmediated experience — knowing by living contact rather than by report; the punishment, Maulana Ali says, is not announced from afar — it is tasted, in the body, fully.
